Assess where predictions extrapolate beyond the data

Source: R/extrapolation.R
assess_extrapolation.Rd

Computes, for each prediction location, indicators of whether a prediction from a fitted geostatistical model relies on extrapolation, either in space (far from the data relative to the estimated spatial correlation) or in the covariates (outside the conditions observed in the data).

Usage

assess_extrapolation(object, newdata, spatial_threshold = 0.8)

Arguments

object

A fitted RiskMap model.

newdata

An sf object of prediction points with the covariates used by the model, typically a grid from create_grid().

spatial_threshold

Share of the spatial variance left unexplained by the data above which a location is classed as spatial extrapolation. Defaults to 0.8.

Value

An sf object of class RiskMap_extrapolation with the rows and geometry of newdata and the columns

covariates_outside

Number of covariates outside their observed range.

covariate_novelty

Largest distance outside an observed range, as a share of that range (0 when all are within range).

most_novel_covariate

Name of the design-matrix column with the largest distance outside its range, or NA.

covariate_leverage

Leverage relative to its maximum over the data.

spatial_unexplained

Share of the spatial variance not explained by the data.

extrapolation

Factor with levels "Supported", "Spatial", "Covariate" and "Spatial and covariate".

Rows with missing covariates have missing indicators. Map the result with plot.RiskMap_extrapolation().

Details

Covariates are assessed on the model's scale, that is, as the columns of the fixed-effect design matrix. A model with log(elevation) is therefore assessed on log elevation, and a spline in age through each of its basis columns. For each column, the distance outside the range observed in the data is expressed as a share of that range.

The leverage \(h(x) = d(x)^\top (D^\top D)^{-1} d(x)\), where \(D\) is the fitted design matrix, is reported relative to its maximum over the data. Values above 1 indicate a combination of covariates that is more unusual than any in the data, even when each covariate is within its range.

The unexplained spatial variance is \(1 - \rho(x)^\top (R + \nu^2 I)^{-1} \rho(x)\), where \(\rho(x)\) holds the estimated correlations between \(x\) and the sampled locations, \(R\) their correlation matrix, and \(\nu^2\) the ratio of the nugget (and, for Gaussian models, the measurement-error variance) to the spatial variance. It is close to 0 next to well-sampled locations and close to 1 where the data carry no information about the spatial effect. Unlike the distance to the nearest sampled location, it accounts for the estimated scale of spatial correlation and for clustering of the sampled locations. It depends only on where the data were collected, not on the outcomes or on the number of individuals at each location. For binomial, Poisson and negative binomial outcomes, which carry less information than a noise-free observation of the linear predictor, it is therefore an optimistic (lower) value.

A location is classed as covariate extrapolation when any covariate lies outside its observed range or its relative leverage exceeds 1, and as spatial extrapolation when its unexplained spatial variance exceeds spatial_threshold. The two are kept separate because they call for different responses: more sampling where data are sparse, and caution about the form of the covariate effects outside the observed conditions.

See also

plot.RiskMap_extrapolation(), predict.RiskMap()

Examples

data(italy_sim)
example_data <- italy_sim[1:50, ]
fit <- glgpm(y ~ log(pop_dens) + gp(), data = example_data,
             family = "gaussian", messages = FALSE)
extrapolation <- assess_extrapolation(fit, italy_sim[51:100, ])
table(extrapolation$extrapolation)
#> 
#>             Supported               Spatial             Covariate 
#>                     0                    40                     0 
#> Spatial and covariate 
#>                    10
